For years, residents of a Southern California beach town could walk a mile along a stretch of cream-colored sand while ocean waves lapped at their feet. That journey has now been cut short.
San Clemente, recognized for nearly a century as a "Spanish village by the sea," is losing its shoreline to erosion. Rising seas and crashing waves have bisected the city's picturesque North Beach, while eroding bluffs threaten waterfront homes and have repeatedly forced the closure of a passenger train route considered the second busiest in the country.
It is one of numerous California coastal communities confronting the effects of sea level rise. Nearly a decade ago, scientists forecast that more than half of Southern California ’s beaches could significantly erode by 2100, radically altering how people live and recreate along the state’s famed coast.
"The constant pressure is sea level rise," said Sean Vitousek, research oceanographer with the U.S. Geological Survey. "It is going to keep rising, and rising, and the beaches will retreat landward."
Following years of erosion, California is preparing for flooding and landslides ahead of this year’s expected super El Niño, a temporary warming in parts of the equatorial Pacific that warps weather worldwide. Already this year, seawater flooded residences in Long Beach near Los Angeles during a hurricane-driven storm surge, and the town of Pacifica south of San Francisco closed its cracked concrete pier. A recent study indicated that El Niño events are strengthening due to human-caused climate change.
In San Clemente, a town of 62,000 people, urban development has restricted the flow of sediment that historically replenished local beaches, while warmer waters drive waves higher and further ashore. The challenge has led residents of the largely Republican city to consider taxing themselves for beach restoration. A measure adding a 1% sales tax to fund wildfire protection and sand replenishment is on the November ballot.
Over the past five years, the rail line operating along the coast for more than a century has faced recurring closures due to encroaching surf on one side and fragile bluffs on the other. The 7-mile (11-kilometer) segment belongs to a 351-mile (565-kilometer) passenger rail corridor connecting San Diego with Los Angeles County's major port complex and San Luis Obispo. It is also used by freight and the military.
Transportation officials have reinforced the tracks to ensure passenger safety by laying down rock. But as waves slam against the rocks, they sweep more sand offshore and accelerate erosion that will eventually threaten the rail line again.
Locals say the erosion is dramatically altering their community.
"We've lost our walkable beach," said Cameron Cosgrove, a San Clemente resident who wrote the tax measure. "It used to be you could come to North Beach, walk the beach trail, or on the beach to the pier and actually all the way down to the south end of town. Can’t do either anymore."
City and transit officials agree more sand is needed and note that coastal communities, including surf hub Huntington Beach, have nourished their beaches for years. Opponents of the measure want sand — but not the tax — and argue San Clemente should work with other communities on a regional approach.
"Fighting Mother Nature is very expensive," said City Councilman Zhen Wu, who opposes the measure.
City Manager Andy Hall said San Clemente faces a sand deficit of about 3 million cubic yards. Getting that much sand to the beach is no easy task, he said, adding that trucking it would require 300,000 trips.
Darrell Johnson, chief executive of the Orange County Transportation Authority, said a challenge has been getting state permits for more sand. He hopes California's recent emergency declaration ahead of El Niño will speed up the process. In the long run, Johnson said officials will study moving trains inland — an idea previously deemed too costly. A third option is to halt the line, he said.
"If we can’t figure out how to shore up properly in a way that is long-term in nature, and we can't figure out how to relocate, I think that is a question that’s going to have to be asked," Johnson said. "'What happens to passenger rail? What happens to freight?'"
Further south, transportation officials have been working to stabilize coastal bluffs to shore up the rail line in the community of Del Mar. The plan is to eventually move the tracks, but officials have not decided where.
Charlie Fox, a 56-year-old San Clemente resident and marine meteorologist, said sand provides a critical buffer between whatever structures — train tracks, homes, lifeguard headquarters — are built along the coast. The lifelong surfer said sand also helps waves roll gently onshore, creating a steady wave break for surfing.
On a recent morning, surfers bobbed in the water off North Beach, not far from the rocky structure shoring up the train tracks by the sea.
"When you see those rocks, that's them attempting to fight the ocean," Fox said. "That is a futile endeavor."
"The ocean wins," he added. "Ocean always eventually wins."

President Donald Trump appeared to intensify his irritation with GOP Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar on Saturday evening after reposting a series of social media attacks on the congresswoman who made waves last week for breaking with him on his immigration tactics.
The president shared in quick succession on Truth Social at least 14 posts from other users critical of Salazar, who is facing a tough reelection race in Florida as Republicans’ midterm fortunes decline.
“She is nothing but a back stabber. I’m glad the Latino support hasn’t wavered,” one user wrote in a post shared by Trump.
Another user slammed the congresswoman: “She wants amnesty for the ppl how criminally crossed our borders defying our laws.”
“So we need a NEW Republican to Replace Salazar,” different user said .
The GOP stampede away from Trump is growing — including in pretty red districts
CNN reached out to the White House and Salazar’s office and reelection campaign for comment on the reposts.
Salazar, who represents a heavily Hispanic district, drew Trump’s ire last week after she broke with the president in a new ad ahead of the midterms. The congresswoman addresses Trump directly in the ad, speaking straight to the camera as she says, “some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far.”
Salazar points to statistics she said show that 50% of the people detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in July “had no criminal record.”
Following the ad’s release, Trump confirmed in response to a question from a reporter that he had seen the ad and still backed the Florida congresswoman, even though he did not share her view.
“I disagree with her,” Trump said in the Oval Office. He claimed that Salazar “got a little bit soft on the border” and wouldn’t have won without his endorsement.

Salazar told “Face The Nation” that she had a “very good conversation” with the president after releasing the campaign ad and characterized Trump as “very receptive” to her warning that Hispanic voters feel “betrayed” ahead of the midterm election.
The congresswoman’s ad comes as ICE increased immigration arrests nationwide over the summer. In August, for example, ICE took around 51,000 people into custody, setting a new high under the second Trump administration. The previous high had been set the month prior when the agency took more than 46,000 people into custody in July.

Major League Baseball has played games in a cornfield, a NASCAR speedway and historic ballparks. Now, the league is apparently wondering whether it can add a national park to the list.
MLB approached the Trump administration about holding a regular-season game in a national park, and National Park Service Deputy Director Frank Lands recently visited Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming to examine three potential locations for a temporary baseball facility, The Washington Post reported.
The idea remains preliminary. No site has been selected and no permits have been issued. The White House stressed that MLB â not President Donald Trump or his administration â proposed the concept.
âThis is not a Presidential directive, nor is it being directed by the White House,â the White House told the Post.
For MLB, playing somewhere unexpected has increasingly become part of the schedule. In addition to international games in England, Australia, Japan, South Korea and Mexico, the league has staged games at Iowaâs âField of Dreamsâ site, historic Rickwood Field and Bristol Motor Speedway, where a temporary baseball field was constructed inside the NASCAR track.
Turning Grand Teton into the next destination could be considerably more complicated.
Hosting tens of thousands of baseball fans inside a national park could require substantial temporary infrastructure beyond the field itself, including facilities for spectators and players, broadcast crews, security, sanitation and emergency services â not to mention getting thousands of people to and from the site.
Those demands could run into Grand Tetonâs rules for special events. Events cannot alter the movement of visitors, wildlife or traffic, close roads or trails, or take place in designated wilderness areas. Commercial logos, banners and tent-like structures are also prohibited.
At least one location examined by Lands is reportedly already-disturbed land used for storage rather than untouched parkland. Conservation advocates have nevertheless raised concerns about the environmental impact and precedent of staging a major professional sporting event inside a national park.

No detailed construction plan or environmental review has been released, leaving unanswered how MLB could stage the game while satisfying those protections.
Even if those hurdles can be cleared, baseball wonât be coming to the Tetons soon. MLBâs 2027 special-event schedule is already set, making 2028 the earliest possible date.

The UFC has issued a statement on the health condition of veteran bantamweight fighter Raoni Barcelos following UFC Vegas 121.
Here is the UFC’s statement in full, which was issued several hours after the conclusion of UFC Vegas 121 :
“Following his fight tonight, Raoni Barcelos was immediately transported to a Level 1 trauma center for evaluation. The hospital medical team conducted a CT scan and comprehensive assessment, and he is currently being monitored. Barcelos is stable, alert and responsive, with full movement. He will remain under medical supervision. We will provide updates on his condition as they become available,” the UFC said in a statement posted on its official website .
Barcelos was up on the scorecards in the main event of UFC Vegas 121 against Raul Rosas Jr., but ended up losing via fifth-round TKO when he suffered some sort of medical emergency in what can only be described as a scary situation .
At first, it appeared that Barcelos may have been knocked out from a takedown, but it soon became clear that something else was happening as he did not appear to be moving, and with the situation being as concerning as it was, he was immediately rushed to a local Las Vegas hospital.
Fans online were understandably frightened by what was playing out on their screen, as it was one of the scariest situations we have ever seen in a UFC fight. Fortunately, it appears that Barcelos is going to be okay .
While Barcelos’s health is obviously of the utmost concern, it is worth mentioning that he put on an absolutely incredible performance against Rosas, as both fighters won $100,000 in bonuses for Fight of the Night.
It is truly unfortunate for Barcelos that he was just a few minutes away from winning his sixth straight fight and picking up arguably the biggest win of his UFC career to date before he suffered the medical emergency.
However, despite the defeat, it was an amazing performance, and one he should be proud to look back on once he gets fully healthy.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Over the past few days, you have probably been hit over the head with stories about rising bond yields.
I hate to admit it, but I even churned out a host of stories on yields this week. Love me a good headline!
The rise in yields is one of the most important things happening in markets right now. Actually, this started in the summer, but you know what I mean.
"I would say [it's] not a crisis but an eye-opener, and it's something I think you've got to think about," BlackRock chief investment officer of global fixed income Rick Rieder said on Yahoo Finance's Sozzi Unleashed .
Rieder was among the finalists for the Fed chair role that ended up going to Kevin Warsh.
But I don't want you to lose focus on the "why" behind the move. It's not because of some warning on the nation's debt from some third-rate investing pundit. That's not the reason at all.
The reason is that the economy is weakening under the tightening grip of inflation. And this is going down just as the Federal Reserve makes it costlier for businesses and you, the consumer, to borrow money.
Here are a few red flags I have picked up on this week that no one is talking about, other than me.
Execs at payroll services company Paychex ( PAYX ) said this week that we are in a low-hire, low-fire environment. Hardly a bullish economic endorsement.
Lucky Charms maker General Mills ( GIS ) warned about more quarters of pressured margins at the hands of a big pickup in inflation in things like wheat, diesel, and packaging. I think this sheds light on what the Fed hawks like New York Fed president John Williams are telling us about rate hikes.
Cracker Barrel ( CBRL ) called out a 6.1% traffic drop in its most recent quarter. Darden ( DRI ) said sales at its Olive Garden chain grew just 1.1% in the quarter. The read: Much higher gas prices are swallowing up the disposable income of many households.
It's always important to know the "why" when it comes to markets — and sadly, the "why" isn't great in the case of yields.

It's all just ahead on Face the Nation.
Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation.
With just weeks to go before the midterm elections, President Trump is facing challenges on multiple fronts, persistent voter concerns about the economy, rising prices for consumers, and growing questions about his strategy in the war with Iran.
Adding to those pressures is an ongoing confrontation with the White House press corps. The major television networks resumed coverage of the president's daily activities after a federal judge ordered the White House to restore access to outlets that had been banned, that only after Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit was already under way. The administration continued to limit CNN's participation in the television pool yesterday.
Regarding the war, President Trump told reporters yesterday he had rejected the latest offer to end it presented by Iranian officials during meetings in New York. But will he keep diplomacy alive or resume strikes? The Pentagon's public casualty count rose again last week, bringing the number of U.S. military deaths to 19.
The Iran conflict is where we begin this morning, a rare network exclusive interview with the leader of a country at war with the United States. We sat down with President Masoud Pezeshkian New York on Friday, and we began by asking him about Iran's latest proposal, built on what was outlined in the memorandum of understanding signed by both sides in June.
MASOUD PEZESHKIAN (Iranian President) (through translator): Now, in fact, there is a framework along the same path, with the same objectives that were established.
Ultimately, the requests that were included in that memorandum and MOU have now been broken down into stages so that we can proceed according to those stages. If the United States agrees to proceed in that way, everything will return to the way it was before, because, right now, it's the United States that has blocked our way.
And, naturally, Iran has also blocked the way from its side. These are things that both sides need to open up first. Then we can sit down at the negotiating table and discuss other issues at hand.
MARGARET BRENNAN: If President Trump accepts this proposal, can you guarantee your military will abide by it?
PRESIDENT MASOUD PEZESHKIAN (through translator): Obviously, we will abide by whatever we commit to.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, President Trump said he was open to meeting with you when you were here. That didn't happen. Would you be willing – if you want direct communication, would you be willing to speak directly with him, to meet with him?
PRESIDENT MASOUD PEZESHKIAN (through translator): Now the atmosphere of distrust that has developed between Iran and the United States is because we have had several rounds of talks with the United States.
Basically, we need to determine now what exactly we want to reach an understanding on. If we don't abide by what we have written down as necessary, can we really resolve it through dialogue? We wrote it down and signed it. It's clear.
The first thing that needs to happen is that the distrust created by this war has to be overcome.
PRESIDENT MASOUD PEZESHKIAN (through translator): We need to abide by what we have written down.
The United States needs to show that it does not intend to overthrow our government or our administration. Put yourself in our position. Imagine someone came and martyred your supreme leader, and then not abide by everything you had agreed upon. What would be your reaction? It's not something that can be resolved that simply.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, the offer that you are making for diplomacy, is it now to begin talks about putting limits on Iran's nuclear program, but not fully abandoning that program?
PRESIDENT MASOUD PEZESHKIAN (through translator): Of course, we agree. We had already reached an understanding on this in our previous talks.
They struck it down. We're not supposed to develop nuclear weapons. Within the framework of the NPT and the other existing frameworks, all of these issues are matters that can be agreed upon. Unfortunately, they are disregarding the rights that international law grants to all countries.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Under international law, including the Non-Proliferation Treaty your country signed, though, inspectors would be allowed in from the U.N. Will you allow them in now to settle those concerns?
PRESIDENT MASOUD PEZESHKIAN (through translator): That is absolutely correct. According to those very international laws, when there are nuclear centers under the inspections and auspices of the IAEA within the NPT framework, no country has the legal right to attack those nuclear centers and sites.
But America and Israel carried out the act of attacking them. Now the agency itself, rather than its strong condemnation, showed absolutely no reaction. Why is it that centers and sites that were completely under their unprecedented surveillance and inspections regime – perhaps they had the most surveillance on those centers.
We had no deviation from that framework. Why did they attack it in the first place?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, the IAEA said they were not being given full access. U.N. inspectors weren't being allowed in. They said they couldn't guarantee the peaceful nature of your program, and say now you have 440 kilograms of 60 percent enriched uranium.
So they want to be able to verify that that won't be made into a weapon. Will your country allow in weapons inspectors now?
PRESIDENT MASOUD PEZESHKIAN (through translator): That is absolutely correct.
This occurred after America chose to tear up the JCPOA. Iran waited for one year in order for the European counterparts to live up to their commitments within the JCPOA. They failed to do so. Iran left the JCPOA and continued on the path that it saw fit.
Now, if they want to come in and have inspections, we can reach accords and agreements vis-a-vis that specific topic within the negotiations, not for them now to come and inspect those existing frameworks again.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And we will hear more from President Pezeshkian later this hour.
But we turn now to Republican Louisiana Senator John Kennedy.
Good morning to you, Senator.

articles.title_zh: What Democrats are getting right – and wrong – in run-up to midterms: ‘We can’t just be anti-Trump’
articles.content_orig:
Grassroots organizer Yasmin Radjy on the Democratic ground game leading into the midterm elections
I n the run-up to the US midterm elections , Swing Left – a grassroots political group focused on electing Democrats to office – has spent time canvassing in dozens of districts across the country to hear from hundreds of thousands of voters.
Now, with fewer than 40 days until the US midterm elections, the group’s executive director, Yasmin Radjy, sets out what she feels Democrats have been getting right and wrong this election cycle, and why these races are vital for the party’s future control of the US Congress in the years to come.
We are now five weeks out. What do you feel have been, and will continue to be, the defining issues of these midterm races?
Yasmin Radjy : The two things head and shoulders above everything else that we’re hearing about: one is a feeling like the system is broken , and soon after that are various issues around cost of living. The two are often related, but there are very few conversations where one or both of those issues are not coming up. Everyone’s gotten the memo that we need to talk about affordability. I don’t think there’s a Republican or a Democrat who’s not aware of that. The candidates who are really standing out this cycle again across the ideological spectrum, from Abdul El-Sayed [in Michigan] to Mary Peltola [in Alaska]. And on the House map, Paige Cognetti [in Pennsylvania], to Amish Shah [in Arizona]. They are connecting those dots in a way that is specific and that is also mirroring the nature of those districts.
What do you think the party needs to focus on to regain trust, and establish a clear sense of identity with voters moving forward – particularly after 2024?
We have to follow up with people when they express urgency around the very real and material concerns that they have. When they express disappointment, we can’t pretend like everything is going great. We also need to acknowledge that a lot of the things we’ve been doing aren’t working. That requires having tough, not just conversations, but introspection, and openness to trying new things, testing new things and taking bigger, riskier swings than we’re accustomed to.
On one of the must-win races you mentioned – the open Senate seat in Michigan – what do you feel voters are responding to with a candidate like Abdul El-Sayed? What do you think he needs to do in order to win over voters in that state that Trump won?
I think something he is modeling is a “talk to everybody and engage with everyone” approach, not just talk to the people who already agree with you. I think he really won his primary because of organizing. In terms of the issues and themes in Michigan, what we’re hearing is very similar to elsewhere with subtle differences: both parties suck, and no politician cares about that voter, their community and people like them. That is ubiquitous. What he is able to speak compellingly on with a lot of authority is his feeling like the system is broken, and he is doing a good job of tying that to affordability and a whole host of other issues.
I’m curious what you think might be the biggest obstacle for Democrats in this cycle? What could be getting in the party’s way?
One is that we continue to not have a sufficiently clear answer, for a time when the winds are not blowing in our direction, of what Democrats stand for besides being anti-Trump. We need to start answering that now – and it’s OK if that answer has shades of difference in Michigan, Alaska and North Carolina. The second piece is we cannot assume our base will be with us again because of anti-Trump sentiment in a way that can sustain durable power.
Something under-discussed that keeps me up at night is if we are not building long-term, durable power, by 2030 we are going to wake up to an election where, if we don’t have power in the states, we will not be able to win congressional majorities because of how bad redistricting will look. Population shifts are clear in California and New York – two big blue states essential for presidential math – and they will be losing electoral college votes starting in 2030. Texas and Florida are the inverse – they are going to gain power. If we don’t treat the midterms as our most important moment to build infrastructure while there’s money pouring in, while there’s energy to have a shot at winning tough Republican seats in a way we can sustain, we are going to lose without question in the future, because we will have squandered an opportunity.
I want to discuss the concerns about progressives, from establishment Democrats. What’s your response to those in the coalition who question whether these progressive candidates have a real shot in battlegrounds that the party wants to either retain or flip?
We have members who are Democratic Socialists of America members. We have members who think DSA is a huge threat to democracy – we’ve got the full gamut. Our perspective is that the fixation on ideology and the DSA-versus-centrist divide is a completely false binary. We need to win a majority, and there is a level of pragmatism among the grassroots that is underappreciated. The binary will crumble, not because it doesn’t exist in our institutions, but because that’s not how voters are . We talk to voters every day who might be DSA-aligned on healthcare and Blue Dog-aligned on the border, and it’s the same person. If we lead with genuine curiosity and openness to listening to voters, we immediately see that voters are idiosyncratic, strange and full of contradictions because they’re human.
Linked to this, I’m thinking about James Talarico [the Democratic nominee for the US Senate seat in Texas] and Rob Sand [the Democratic gubernatorial nominee in Iowa]. They are showing a pivot in their messaging, particularly when it comes to trans rights. Do you feel that is a necessary strategy right now to court those swing voters, independents and moderates in newly competitive battleground states?
I think when you go out and really talk to people, specifically on the issue of trans rights, most Americans want trans people to have rights – and the areas of discomfort range from lack of knowledge. Their worldview on trans issues is curated by Fox News, so there is an information gap. Most voters, including many Democrats, have complicated feelings about the trans people in sports issue. The answer is not to start repeating Fox News talking points. The way to talk about these issues – and this is what the data shows – is to break down the pieces: all Americans want every American to have a certain set of freedoms. The trans and sports issue is complicated, and it is not really a decision for governments, it’s a decision for the leagues.
I think Sarah McBride is a perfect example of this – leading with grace, recognizing that changing hearts and minds takes time, and that people use clunky language along the way.
Looking ahead, do you think Democrats are doing enough to respond to Donald Trump’s efforts to undermine elections in this cycle in particular?
I would say there is an asymmetric investment in election protection right now. And that asymmetric investment is on the litigation front, it is on the donor-organizing and on the grassroots-organizing fronts. And I feel really confident and really relieved, candidly, that the amount of investment of time, talent and strategy has been placed on that. The flip side is the progressive ecosystem, overall, has not invested as much in the actual act of winning the election, and there is nothing more important for election protection than winning each competitive race by a big enough margin that Trump doesn’t have the incentive to try any kind of funny business. We are not where we should be in some of the most competitive races in the country in terms of dollars invested and volunteers ready to help that candidate, and to me, that is the most essential ingredient to election protection.

A popular story about a lesbian bar in Massachusetts has gone so viral that Hollywood studios are now considering potential adaptations for the article , according to an industry report.
On September 22, the Boston Globe published the piece in question , titled "A Western Mass. lesbian bar required KN-95 masks. When it changed the rules, all hell broke loose." The article, written by Annalisa Quinn, quickly became a hot topic on social media feeds and sparked online discussions and think pieces on all corners of the internet — and the buzzy conversation has apparently made its way over to film and TV executives.
According to a new report from The Hollywood Reporter , talent agency UTA "has been fielding inquiries about potential adaptations for the article — both in the scripted space and the documentary sphere." UTA represents the Globe.
A spokesperson for the newspaper told THR : "This story has certainly resonated with a wide range of audiences nationally and internationally. It is now one of the most-read stories we've published, and has already garnered many thousands of subscriptions."
The Independent has reached out to the Globe and UTA for comment.
The Boston Globe is reportedly fielding inquiries regarding a potential adaptation of its recent viral article (Getty Images)
The article follows a lesbian establishment, Last Ditch Bar, in Greenfield, Massachusetts, that faced chaos after lifting its mask mandate.
Bartenders announced in an Instagram post issued to the "immunocompromised disabled divas" in August that patrons no longer had to wear KN95 masks on Saturday nights.
The decision was met with backlash and accused of being "complicit in a mass disabling event."
Quinn's article was praised online for its relaying of the dramatic saga, which was complete with zinger one-liner quotes from scorned customers as well as sympathetic details about the bar owner who is in a mountain of debt because of the crisis.
2015 movie 'Spotlight' was based on the Boston Globe's investigative reporting (Kerry Hayes)
It quickly became one of the most read stories in the newspaper's history, with a leaked staffer memo reporting that more than a thousand new subscribers flocked to the Globe in less than a day after the story was published.
The viral article's success is notable considering the stark contrast in subject matter of other monumental articles in the Globe 's history that have been adapted.
In the early 2000s, the newspaper published a Pulitzer Prize-winning series of bombshell articles that exposed the systemic cover-up of abuse within the Catholic Church. The journalism inspired the 2015 Academy Award-winning film Spotlight .
Years later, the paper's investigative reporting on the crimes and death of former New England Patriots star Aaron Hernandez also led to the podcast Gladiator: Aaron Hernandez . The podcast eventually led to scripted FX series American Sports Story: Aaron Hernandez, which was executive produced by Ryan Murphy.

WASHINGTON — A divided Supreme Court has cleared the way for President Trump to finish building his new White House ballroom with mostly private money and without approval from Congress.
By a 5-4 vote, the justices granted an emergency appeal from Trump and his lawyers on Monday, setting aside a judge’s order that would stop the construction.
But Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. dissented, along with the court’s three liberals.
Roberts said the construction project was “likely unlawful” and should not be allowed to continue.
“The White House is not just any building ... when it comes to historic preservation,” Roberts wrote. “Winston Churchill once remarked that ‘[w]e shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us.’ All the more reason to ensure that those responsible follow the rules in deciding what to tear down and what to build up at the People’s House.”
The outcome turned on the standing of the plaintiffs, the National Trust for Historic Preservation and its members.
The conservative majority pointed to Alison Hoagland, one of its members, who said she lives in Washington, walks by the White House about once a month and said she found the “scale,” “height” and “massing” of the huge ballroom to be distasteful.
“This court has not found standing in circumstances like these before. To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury,” the unsigned order said.
Trump has responded to growing legal and political obstacles to his ballroom, arch and other projects by attempting to force approvals through faster than opponents can challenge them.
It is a major victory for Trump, whose ballroom project has become a signature effort of his second term and a political lightning rod in Washington, where Republicans have refused to fund it with public money.
Trump celebrated the victory with a post on social media, declaring the venue would now be built “without any further contingency, doubt, or threat.”
“We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C.,” Trump wrote. “When completed in the Summer of 2028, the magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex will be something that the entire Country is very proud of.”
The massive new structure, set to dwarf the historic White House mansion, is the president’s singular vision — one of a string of aesthetic projects Trump has pursued in a feverish effort to cement his legacy by putting his personal stamp on the nation’s capital.
But preservationists and architects have criticized the proposed ballroom as a garish, rushed project that ignored the input of experts. The president has personally overruled his own chosen architects after being told the building would overwhelm the executive complex.
Democrats have seized on the president’s fixation on the ballroom as a symbol of vanity and detachment from the concerns of everyday Americans heading into November’s midterm elections.
According to recent polls, a bipartisan majority of voters disapprove of the president’s handling of the economy and say the country is facing an affordability crisis. The ballroom is projected to cost more than $400 million, excluding the undisclosed cost of underground security upgrades.
Trump’s three appointees — Justices Neil M. Gorsuch, Brett M. Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — joined conservative Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel A. Alito in an unsigned opinion ruling for the president.
The conservative majority also said Trump and his appointees had stressed the new ballroom was needed for national security and said the lower courts judges should not have interfered.
California officials stressed that the court’s ruling does not allow final implementation of the new rules requested by Trump.
Administration officials have argued that an underground “integrated military complex” was the heart of the project and that the ballroom would merely be sit top of the facility “vitally required by national security.”
The decision is not a final ruling, but it gives a green light to Trump’s go-it-alone approach, which is in keeping with his history as a hotel builder.
He believed the White House needed a grand ballroom that could seat hundreds of dignitaries. Acting on his own, he ordered the East Wing torn down in October to make room of his larger ballroom.
He also said most of the project would be paid for by private donations.
But the Constitution gave Congress the power to manage property belonging to the United States. A 1912 law says new buildings “shall not erected ... on public grounds within the District of Columbia without express authority of Congress.”
Trump chose to ignore the law and did not seek approval from Congress, which is led by Republicans.
The Republican president’s lawyers had asked the justices to reconsider their refusal to hear his appeal. The court denied Trump’s petition along with several others.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued in December, contending Trump was a “temporary tenant, not the owner” of the White House.
U.S. District Judge Richard Leon ruled Trump had no authority to build a ballroom on the White House grounds without the approval of Congress, and he ordered a halt to the above-ground construction.
The District of Columbia Circuit Court affirmed his decision by a 2-1 vote.
“Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People’s House — to fit a particular President’s desires,” wrote Judge Patricia Millett for the appeals court.
Trump’s lawyers sent a fast-track appeal to the Supreme Court on Aug. 14.
The court’s majority allowed Trump to fend off the legal challenge by concluding the historic preservationists could not show they were harmed by  the huge new ballroom.

UFC fighter Raoni Barcelos was hospitalized at a Level 1 trauma center in the aftermath of Saturday's loss to Raul Rosas Jr.
UFC released a statement that said Barcelos was "stable, alert and responsive, with full movement" after undergoing a CT scan.
As ESPN's Jeff Wagenheim described, Barcelos "appeared to lose consciousness after a fifth-round takedown and was carried from the cage on a stretcher" at the end of the UFC Fight Night matchup in Las Vegas.
Wagenheim noted Barcelos' coach, Davi Ramos, provided an update on Saturday as well and said, "everything is fine, everyone can stay calm."
As for the fight itself, Rosas was trailing heading into the final round but was more aggressive toward the end. After he slammed Barcelos to the mat, the referee stopped the fight when it seemed as if the 39-year-old was unconscious.
Rosas, who became the youngest fighter to ever sign with UFC at 17 years old in 2022, has now won six fights in a row.
However, he was focused on his opponent in the aftermath as well.
"I want everybody tonight to please pray for Raoni Barcelos," he said in his postfight interview to the crowd. "Man, he's a warrior. It takes two to tango."
UFC's statement said Barcelos "will remain under medical supervision. We will provide updates on his condition as they become available."

The outcome of the 2026 election will be determined primarily by how well Republicans play defense across the growing list of GOP-held House and Senate seats Democrats are targeting. But the GOP is also hoping to play offense by flipping some House and Senate seats Democrats now control.
Because of their redistricting maneuvers, Republicans have more opportunities to flip House seats held by the other side than is typical for the president’s party in midterm elections. In the Senate, Republicans are seriously targeting four Democratic-held seats. But in both chambers, the same collapse in President Donald Trump’s approval rating that is threatening so many GOP incumbents is dimming the party’s prospects of unseating many Democrats.
The Republican financial advantage is large enough that the party can afford to force Democrats to commit resources defending seats they now hold — which is itself a benefit for the GOP. But it has never been easy during a midterm for the president’s party to flip seats held by the other side. And that has been especially true in midterms defined by a wave of discontent with the president’s performance — the conditions that appear to be coalescing this year.
Over nearly the past five decades, the party holding the White House has faced five full-scale wipeouts in House elections. Each time, while losing dozens of their own House seats, the president’s party has struggled to oust many legislators on the other side.
The president’s party flipped no more than four House seats held by the other side during the “wave” midterm elections under Ronald Reagan in 1982, Bill Clinton in 1994, Barack Obama in 2010 and Trump in 2018. In 2006, while losing the House under George W. Bush, Republicans did not capture a single Democratic-held seat. (Amid the more modest Democratic House losses in 2022 under Joe Biden, the party flipped four Republican-held seats.)
Republicans have legitimate reason to expect they can improve on that humble record this year. The National Republican Congressional Committee is officially targeting three dozen Democratic-held seats.
In this environment, Democrats don’t worry too much about Republicans defeating any of the dozen Democrats they are targeting in districts that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024. The major House race forecasters also generally give the GOP modest odds in those seats.
The core of this year’s GOP pick-up opportunity is the 22 Democrats running in seats that voted for Trump in 2024 . About two-thirds of those seats are in states where Republicans have redrawn the congressional maps to improve their chances.
After that gerrymandering offensive, the number of Democrats in Trump-won seats this year will roughly equal the 23 House Republicans who ran in 2018 in seats that voted for Hillary Clinton two years earlier.
Tracking states’ unprecedented redistricting efforts
In 2018, Democrats beat 20 of those 23 Clinton-district Republicans. That precedent undergirds the Republican optimism about flipping more seats than usual. “In 2018, Democrats took back their own turf,” says Mike Marinella, press secretary for the NRCC. “Now, in 2026, it’s almost the exact same situation on the other side as Democrats are the ones renting districts in Trump country, and we’re going all in to bring Republican voters home in November.”
But Republicans face many hurdles trying to match the overpowering Democratic 2018 performance in split-ticket districts. The GOP is strongly favored this year in the six seats where the new lines are forcing Democrats to run in districts that gave Trump about 57% of the vote or more (though Democrats and some independent analysts don’t entirely rule out an upset from Democratic incumbents Shomari Figures in Alabama and Darren Soto in Florida, or in an open seat around Houston).
The remaining 16 Democrats running in seats Trump won with 55% of the vote or less, though, are proving more competitive than many analysts initially expected. In 2018, Democrats looking to oust Republicans in districts that voted for Clinton had a huge tailwind of dissatisfaction with Trump. Conversely, Republicans looking to oust Democrats in districts that voted for Trump now face the headwind of discontent with the president.
CJ Warnke, communications director for House Majority PAC, the principal Democratic super PAC investing in House races, says that in the group’s polling, Trump’s approval rating “is underwater across the board, to varying degrees, in every district across the battlefield.” And that means even in districts Trump carried in 2024, association with him may be more anchor than sail in 2026.
The three heavily Latino South Texas Congressional districts that Republicans redrew in their gerrymander captures the GOP’s challenge. State Republicans reconfigured the Rio Grande Valley seats held by Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez and another Democratic seat south of San Antonio so that all three became districts where Trump carried about 55% of the vote in 2024 amid his sweeping gains among Latino voters.
But Trump’s support has eroded across the region. Recent polling by Texas Southern University found that about 55% of voters now disapprove of his performance in both the Cuellar and Gonzalez districts. (The poll didn’t include the San Antonio-area district.)
“It’s pretty obvious to anybody that does a poll that… the president’s popularity in South Texas is surely not what it was two years ago,” says Republican consultant Wayne Hamilton, who runs Project Red TX, an organization dedicated to growing the party in South Texas.
While Trump’s moves to regain control of the southern border have widely received good marks across South Texas, his aggressive deportation drive has generated bitter backlash. Probably even more damaging has been the increase in fuel prices driven by the Iran war.
Johnny Garcia, a sheriff’s deputy in Bexar County who is the Democratic nominee for the San Antonio-area House seat, used Spanish slang for trucks when he noted in an interview that for many Latino men, a “fancy troquita , with their 30-inch jacked-up tires and their loud mufflers” is a source of great pride. “And now,” Garcia added, “we’re seeing, under this administration, that troquita is being parked in the driveway, and they’re being forced to drive their wives’ minivans, because they don’t have the money to afford to fill up that gas tank.”
Hamilton said that amid frustration over the economy and immigration enforcement the best asset for Republicans in these seats will be to remind voters why they rejected Democrats in 2024. “People do not want to go back to that,” Hamilton says. “Republicans have to work to… show (voters) your life is better because Republicans restored law and order on the border and promoted economic development.”
But orienting voters to what they didn’t like about Biden may be difficult when they are so frustrated with conditions under Trump. Mark Jones, a Rice University political scientist who helps manage the Texas Southern poll, says the gerrymander was built on the misguided assumption that Trump’s strong 2024 performance in South Texas represented a reliable new baseline for the GOP. Instead, Jones says, “what we are seeing now across Texas is a reversion to where Republicans normally are with Latino voters, which is winning about 40% of the vote.”
In that environment, most independent analysts consider Cuellar and Gonzalez favorites for reelection, with Garcia, while still an underdog, retaining a plausible chance at an upset.

articles.title_orig: Ruby on Rails Creator Declares 'Pencils Down' on Handwritten Code
articles.title_zh: Ruby on Rails Creator Declares 'Pencils Down' on Handwritten Code
articles.content_orig:
A coding legend is waving goodbye to handwritten code.
David Heinemeier Hansson — commonly known as DHH — is the creator of the popular webapp framework Ruby on Rails. He also runs the software company 37signals, where he just instituted a new rule: "We're done writing code by hand."
"We are going, and have gone, pencils down," Hansson said during the Rails World keynote.
At his software company, 37signals, Hansson said that hand-writing code was an "exceptional state," only to be performed when something went wrong with the AI-generated code.
When an AI agent isn't able to produce what the engineers want, they can "get the old pencil out and dot it down for them," Hansson said — but then they "fix the machine."
"This is a recognition of what is already happening," he said.
Indeed, coding has radically transformed in the last year, thanks to AI tools like OpenAI's Codex, Anthropic's Claude Code, and Cursor.
Some developers call coding agents exhilarating, and they stay up late into the night to build with them. Others call AI coding a lonely or tiresome process .
What do engineers actually think? Business Insider polled over 150 software engineers in January about the rise of vibe coding. Over 45% of respondents said they felt they were "keeping up" with AI tools. 17.5% of respondents said they were opting out of using AI code-editing tools entirely.
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
There's only one "serious question" in this moment of coding, Hansson said at the keynote: how to best reap the rewards of AI. "Every other question is below that in the stack of values," he said.
Hansson surveyed the audience: "How many people here are still writing material amounts of code by hand on a weekly basis?"
After watching the crowd, Hansson let out an expletive. "That's about five," he said.
